Queen (Danaus gilippus) butterflies mating for several minutes in the Mojave/Colorado desert at Desert StrawHouse Native Plant Nursery in Sky Valley. 

Queen (Danaus gilippus) and Monarch (Danaus plexippus) are both butterflies in the Tiger Milkweed Butterflies (Danaus) genus. Queen is smaller and has many smaller white spots on wing margins. Queen butterflies flap their wings more than the larger Monarchs that tend to glide.

My favorite Queen (Danaus gilippus) butterfly observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=51743&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1
Two in Tandem: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/330516727

Striated Queen (Danaus gilippus ssp. thersippus) is the subspecies in this region. It is found in the Western U.S, Mexico, and Central America.

BugGuide: https://www.bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Danaus%20gilippus%20thersippus

Queen (Danaus gilippus) is a North and South American butterfly in the Tiger Milkweed Butterflies (Genus Danaus) and the Brush-footed Butterflies (Nymphalidae) family. It has a wingspan of 80–85 mm (2.75--3.5 inches). It looks similar to Monarch (Danaus plexippus), especially when wings are folded, but it is smaller and more reddish-brown above. Queen can be found in meadows, fields, marshes, deserts, and in dry tropical forest edges. The male has a black scent patch on its dorsal hindwings. These pheromones are necessary to attract the female. Monarch and Queen are both in the Tiger Milkweed Butterflies (Danaus) genus.

"Butterflies of the genus Danaus (monarchs, queens, tigers, wanderers, and others) are globally distributed milkweed butterflies recognized for their bright orange-and-black coloration, chemical defense from milkweed toxins, and in some species, long-distance migrations. The genus includes 12–13 recognized species found worldwide, with centers of diversity in North and South America, Africa, and Asia. Well-known representatives include the Monarch (Danaus plexippus), Queen (D. gilippus), Plain Tiger (D. chrysippus), and Common Tiger (D. genutia). Species occupy habitats ranging from tropical lowlands to temperate grasslands, depending on the availability of milkweed (Asclepiadoideae) host plants. Most species show orange to reddish wings with black veins and borders, often with white spots, a classic aposematic signal warning predators of toxicity. Males often have androconial patches (scent scales) on the hindwings used in courtship. Wingspans typically range from 7–12 cm, with the Monarch among the largest. Caterpillars are banded in black, white, and yellow, with pairs of fleshy filaments at both ends. Larvae feed on milkweeds, sequestering cardenolides (cardiac glycosides). These compounds render both larvae and adults toxic or unpalatable to vertebrate predators. Bright coloration functions as a warning signal, reinforced by predator learning. The Monarch is unique for its multi-generational, long-distance migration (up to 3,000 km) between North America and overwintering sites in Mexico or coastal California. Other species, such as D. erippus in South America, show regional movements but not the same scale of migration. Females lay eggs singly on milkweed leaves; larvae undergo complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult). The genus belongs to family Nymphalidae (brush-footed butterflies), tribe Danaini (milkweed butterflies). Historically divided into subgenera (Danaus, Anosia, Salatura), it is now treated as a single genus. Adults visit a wide range of nectar sources, aiding pollination. Monarch declines highlight broader threats to pollinators from habitat loss, pesticides, and climate change. Danaus species participate in Müllerian mimicry rings, where multiple toxic species share similar warning patterns, reinforcing predator avoidance. Danaus butterflies are defined by milkweed dependence, chemical defense, warning coloration, and in some cases, long-distance migration, serving as both ecological keystones and flagship species for conservation."

Brush-footed Butterflies, a.k.a. Four-footed Butterflies, (Nymphalidae):
Brush‑footed butterflies make up the largest butterfly family on Earth, with more than 6,000 species found on every continent except Antarctica. They belong to the superfamily Papilionoidea and include many familiar butterflies such as Monarchs, Admirals, Emperors, and Fritillaries. Because the family is so large, its members show an enormous range of colors, wing shapes, and behaviors.
Adult brush‑footed butterflies have these features: Their front pair of legs is greatly reduced in size and covered with fine, brush‑like hairs. These legs are usually held tucked against the body, so the butterfly appears to stand and walk on only four legs. Many species rest with their upper wings spread flat, showing bold colors and patterns used for warning, display, or camouflage. In contrast, the undersides of the wings are often duller or patterned like bark or leaves, helping the butterfly blend into its surroundings when it closes its wings. Caterpillars in this family vary from smooth‑skinned species, like Monarchs, to others that carry spines, bumps, or horn‑like projections on the head. These structures can help deter predators or break up the caterpillar’s outline. Their chrysalids (a.k.a. pupa) are just as diverse. Many species, including Monarchs, form pupae with metallic‑looking gold or silver spots. These shiny patches may help scatter light, disguise the chrysalis, or signal toxicity, depending on the species. Together, these traits—reduced forelegs, striking wing patterns, varied caterpillar defenses, and often metallic pupae—make the brush‑footed butterflies one of the most distinctive and successful butterfly families in the world.

Monarch (Danaus plexippus) is a large butterfly in the Brush-footed Butterflies (Nymphalidae) family and the Milkweed Butterflies (Danainae) subfamily.
Conservation Status: Imperiled (N2N3) in United States (NatureServe)

eButterfly: https://www.e-butterfly.org/ebapp/en/species/profile/307

MALE vrs FEMALE Wing Pattern:
Male and female Monarch butterflies look similar at first glance, but their wings carry a few reliable clues that separate them. Both sexes have the same basic pattern: deep orange wings crossed by black veins, a black border, and a row of white spots around the edge. The differences show up when you look more closely at the hindwings and the thickness of the veins.
MALE: has scent gland (one small black spot) on each hindwing near abdomen. Example: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/272052495. These 2 spots are scent glands used to release chemical signals during courtship. The veins on a male’s wings are also slightly thinner.
FEMALE: has NO scent gland (a small black spot) on each hindwing near abdomen. Example: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/339176390. Instead, her wing veins are thicker and darker, giving her wings a more heavily lined appearance.

Monarch (Danaus plexippus) in Monterey County CA: Every fall, Monarch butterfies make long-distance migrations from areas that freeze to overwinter along the Pacific coast. This year's overwintering monarchs are the great-grandchildren of the butterflies that left last spring. Over the course of a year, about 4 generations of monarch butterflies breed and reproduce. They follow the growth of native milkweed, which is the only plant their caterpillars will eat. At night and when it's cold and windy, hundreds of monarchs will cluster together in large trees, especially in Eucalyptus and Monterey Pines. The clustering creates an effect like roof shingles, shedding rain and blocking wind. It may also give some protection from predators. Thousands Roosting in Pacific Grove CA: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/189621420

Butterflies of Monterey County: A comprehensive guide to finding and identifying 91 species of butterflies in Monterey County, Chris Tenney and Jan Austin, August 2023, pp. 148-149

Butterflies Through Binoculars: The West: a field guide to the butterflies of western North America, by Jeffrey Glassberg, 2001, pp. 214-215

Butterflies and Moths of North America: https://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species/Danaus-plexippus
Monarch (Danaus plexippus) "Wing Span: 3 3/8 - 4 7/8 inches (8.6 - 12.4 cm). Identification: Upperside of male is bright orange with wide black borders and black veins; hindwing has a patch of scent scales. Upperside of female is orange-brown with wide black borders and blurred black veins. Both sexes have white spots on borders and apex. Life History: Adults warm up by basking dorsally (with their wings open and toward the sun). Female lays a single egg at a time under host milkweed leaves and stems, then caterpillars eat young leaves and flowers. Adults make massive migrations from August-October, flying thousands of miles south to hibernate along the California coast and into central Mexico. A few overwinter along the Gulf coast or south Atlantic coast. Along the way, Monarchs stop to feed on flower nectar and to roost together at night. At the Mexico wintering sites, butterflies roost in trees and form huge aggregations that may have millions of individuals. During the winter the butterflies may take moisture and flower nectar during warm days. Most have mated before they leave for the north in the spring, and females lay eggs along the way. Residents of tropical areas do not migrate but appear to make altitude changes during the dry season.
Flight: In North America during spring and summer there may be 1-3 broods in the north and 4-6 broods in the south. May breed all year in Florida, South Texas, and southeastern California. Caterpillar Hosts: All species of native Milkweeds, including Rush Milkweed (Asclepas subdulata) in the Coachella Valley CA, Common Milkweed (A. syriaca), Swamp Milkweed (A. incarnata), Showy Milkweed (A. speciosa), and others. Most milkweeds contain cardiac glycosides which are stored in the bodies of both the caterpillar and adult. These poisons are distasteful and emetic to birds and other vertebrate predators. After tasting a Monarch, a predator might associate the bright warning colors of the adult or caterpillar with an unpleasant meal, and avoid Monarchs in the future. Adult Food: Nectar from all milkweeds. Early in the season before milkweeds bloom, Monarchs visit a variety of flowers including those in Dogbane family, Lantanas, and Thistles. Habitat: Many open habitats where Milkweed grows, including fields, meadows, weedy areas, marshes, and along roadsides. Range: Southern Canada south through all of the United States, Central America, and most of South America. Also present in Australia, Hawaii, and other Pacific Islands.
Conservation: Overwintering sites in California and Mexico should be protected and conserved."

eButterfly: https://www.e-butterfly.org/ebapp/en/species/profile/307

MALE vrs FEMALE Wing Pattern:
Male and female Monarch butterflies look similar at first glance, but their wings carry a few reliable clues that separate them. Both sexes have the same basic pattern: deep orange wings crossed by black veins, a black border, and a row of white spots around the edge. The differences show up when you look more closely at the hindwings and the thickness of the veins.
MALE: has scent gland (one small black spot) on each hindwing near abdomen. Example: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/272052495. These 2 spots are scent glands used to release chemical signals during courtship. The veins on a male’s wings are also slightly thinner.
FEMALE: has NO scent gland (a small black spot) on each hindwing near abdomen. Example: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/339176390. Instead, her wing veins are thicker and darker, giving her wings a more heavily lined appearance.

Monarch (Danaus plexippus) in Monterey County CA: Every fall, Monarch butterfies make long-distance migrations from areas that freeze to overwinter along the Pacific coast. This year's overwintering monarchs are the great-grandchildren of the butterflies that left last spring. Over the course of a year, about 4 generations of monarch butterflies breed and reproduce. They follow the growth of native milkweed, which is the only plant their caterpillars will eat. At night and when it's cold and windy, hundreds of monarchs will cluster together in large trees, especially in Eucalyptus and Monterey Pines. The clustering creates an effect like roof shingles, shedding rain and blocking wind. It may also give some protection from predators. Monarch (Danaus plexippus) "Wing Span: 3 3/8 - 4 7/8 inches (8.6 - 12.4 cm). Identification: Upperside of male is bright orange with wide black borders and black veins; hindwing has a patch of scent scales. Upperside of female is orange-brown with wide black borders and blurred black veins. Both sexes have white spots on borders and apex. Life History: Adults warm up by basking dorsally (with their wings open and toward the sun). Female lays a single egg at a time under host milkweed leaves and stems, then caterpillars eat young leaves and flowers. Adults make massive migrations from August-October, flying thousands of miles south to hibernate along the California coast and into central Mexico. A few overwinter along the Gulf coast or south Atlantic coast. Along the way, Monarchs stop to feed on flower nectar and to roost together at night. At the Mexico wintering sites, butterflies roost in trees and form huge aggregations that may have millions of individuals. During the winter the butterflies may take moisture and flower nectar during warm days. Most have mated before they leave for the north in the spring, and females lay eggs along the way. Residents of tropical areas do not migrate but appear to make altitude changes during the dry season.
Flight: In North America during spring and summer there may be 1-3 broods in the north and 4-6 broods in the south. May breed all year in Florida, South Texas, and southeastern California. Caterpillar Hosts: All species of native Milkweeds, including Rush Milkweed (Asclepas subdulata) in the Coachella Valley CA, Common Milkweed (A. syriaca), Swamp Milkweed (A. incarnata), Showy Milkweed (A. speciosa), and others. Most milkweeds contain cardiac glycosides which are stored in the bodies of both the caterpillar and adult. These poisons are distasteful and emetic to birds and other vertebrate predators. After tasting a Monarch, a predator might associate the bright warning colors of the adult or caterpillar with an unpleasant meal, and avoid Monarchs in the future. Adult Food: Nectar from all milkweeds. Early in the season before milkweeds bloom, Monarchs visit a variety of flowers including those in Dogbane family, Lantanas, and Thistles. Habitat: Many open habitats where Milkweed grows, including fields, meadows, weedy areas, marshes, and along roadsides. Range: Southern Canada south through all of the United States, Central America, and most of South America. Also present in Australia, Hawaii, and other Pacific Islands.
Conservation: Overwintering sites in California and Mexico should be protected and conserved."

"Butterflies of the genus Danaus (monarchs, queens, tigers, wanderers, and others) are globally distributed milkweed butterflies recognized for their bright orange-and-black coloration, chemical defense from milkweed toxins, and in some species, long-distance migrations. The genus includes 12–13 recognized species found worldwide, with centers of diversity in North and South America, Africa, and Asia. Well-known representatives include the Monarch (Danaus plexippus), Queen (D. gilippus), Plain Tiger (D. chrysippus), and Common Tiger (D. genutia). Species occupy habitats ranging from tropical lowlands to temperate grasslands, depending on the availability of milkweed (Asclepiadoideae) host plants. Most species show orange to reddish wings with black veins and borders, often with white spots, a classic aposematic signal warning predators of toxicity. Males often have androconial patches (scent scales) on the hindwings used in courtship. Wingspans typically range from 7–12 cm, with the Monarch among the largest. Caterpillars are banded in black, white, and yellow, with pairs of fleshy filaments at both ends. Larvae feed on milkweeds, sequestering cardenolides (cardiac glycosides). These compounds render both larvae and adults toxic or unpalatable to vertebrate predators. Bright coloration functions as a warning signal, reinforced by predator learning. The Monarch is unique for its multi-generational, long-distance migration (up to 3,000 km) between North America and overwintering sites in Mexico or coastal California. Other species, such as D. erippus in South America, show regional movements but not the same scale of migration. Females lay eggs singly on milkweed leaves; larvae undergo complete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult). The genus belongs to family Nymphalidae (brush-footed butterflies), tribe Danaini (milkweed butterflies). Historically divided into subgenera (Danaus, Anosia, Salatura), it is now treated as a single genus. Adults visit a wide range of nectar sources, aiding pollination. Monarch declines highlight broader threats to pollinators from habitat loss, pesticides, and climate change. Danaus species participate in Müllerian mimicry rings, where multiple toxic species share similar warning patterns, reinforcing predator avoidance. Danaus butterflies are defined by milkweed dependence, chemical defense, warning coloration, and in some cases, long-distance migration, serving as both ecological keystones and flagship species for conservation."

Brush-footed Butterflies, a.k.a. Four-footed Butterflies, (Nymphalidae):
Brush‑footed butterflies make up the largest butterfly family on Earth, with more than 6,000 species found on every continent except Antarctica. They belong to the superfamily Papilionoidea and include many familiar butterflies such as Monarchs, Admirals, Emperors, and Fritillaries. Because the family is so large, its members show an enormous range of colors, wing shapes, and behaviors.
Adult brush‑footed butterflies have these features: Their front pair of legs is greatly reduced in size and covered with fine, brush‑like hairs. These legs are usually held tucked against the body, so the butterfly appears to stand and walk on only four legs. Many species rest with their upper wings spread flat, showing bold colors and patterns used for warning, display, or camouflage. In contrast, the undersides of the wings are often duller or patterned like bark or leaves, helping the butterfly blend into its surroundings when it closes its wings. Caterpillars in this family vary from smooth‑skinned species, like Monarchs, to others that carry spines, bumps, or horn‑like projections on the head. These structures can help deter predators or break up the caterpillar’s outline. Their chrysalids (a.k.a. pupa) are just as diverse. Many species, including Monarchs, form pupae with metallic‑looking gold or silver spots. These shiny patches may help scatter light, disguise the chrysalis, or signal toxicity, depending on the species. Together, these traits—reduced forelegs, striking wing patterns, varied caterpillar defenses, and often metallic pupae—make the brush‑footed butterflies one of the most distinctive and successful butterfly families in the world.
